newsitem.title: INDIA: Indian Premier Gujral wins vote of confidence.
newsitem.headline: Indian Premier Gujral wins vote of confidence.

text.p: Indian Prime Minister Inder Kumar Gujral won a vote of confidence in parliament on Tuesday, a day after his centre-left government took office.

The speaker of the lower house, P.A. Sangma, announced that Gujral, the fourth prime minister in a year, had won the voice vote at the end of more than 10 hours of debate broadcast on national television.
Gujral's victory had been expected. He had the support of both his 15-party United Front coalition, with 178 votes in the 542-member lower house, and the Congress party with 140.

Congress had helped to topple Gujral's predecessor, H.D. Deve Gowda, in a vote of confidence on April 11, but pledged to support a new centre-left government provided it found a new leader. Gujral was chosen by the United Front as its leader on Saturday and sworn in on Monday.
Gujral, 77, was opposed by the Hindu nationalist Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP), which with its allies controls 193 votes and is the single biggest party in parliament.

The Congress party, which triggered Deve Gowda's fall after withdrawing support for his 10-month-old government, promised to back Gujral for the remaining four years of the Lok Sabha, but with conditions.

Former finance minister Manmohan Singh, the Congress party's economic policy advisor, told Reuters that Gujral's tenure hinged on the success of a coordination committee set up by the two quarrelling allies to sort out policy differences.
Singh said Congress would not seek any changes in the budget proposals for fiscal 1997/98 (April-March) presented by former United Front finance minister P. Chidambaram.
"Reports that we are seeking to change the budget are wrong and baseless," Singh said. "I see no problem in the passage of the budget."
But he said economic policy was one of the key issues to be discussed by the Congress-United Front coordination committee, headed by Gujral and Congress president Sitaram Kesri.
"I think the government will last as long as the coordination mechanism works, and I hope it works for four years," Singh said moments before Gujral moved the confidence motion in parliament.
The BJP said the new government would be short-lived.
"There is already a serious rift over Chidambaram," former BJP finance minister Jaswant Singh told Reuters.

He was referring to the decision by Chidambaram's regional Tamil Maanila Congress party to stay out of the government after its leader G.K. Moopanar was passed over in the leadership tussle last week.
BJP leaders said they would oppose passage of Chidambaram's finance bill, supported by the new government and due to be taken up for discussion on April 30.
"I don't think this government will last beyond 1997," former BJP interior minister Murli Manohar Joshi said.
